solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Sober? Drink punch!

blocks.note: to down a drink is to swallow it in one
to punch someone is to beat them

explanation.surface: Someone is told to stay off the booze, and answers with a call for a bowl of punch.
explanation.walkthrough: Both 'Drink' and 'punch' look like nouns in the surface, but each is a verb here, and 'Sober' is an adjective meaning serious rather than not drunk.
explanation.definitionFit: A sober mood is gloomy and subdued, and downbeat describes exactly that pessimistic, unexcited outlook.

clue.text: Strip clubs opening from tomorrow

indicators.note: an opening is where something starts, so only the initial letter is kept

blocks.note: dives are seedy nightclubs or bars
the first letter of tomorrow

explanation.surface: An announcement that the town's strip clubs will open for business tomorrow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Strip clubs' reads as one phrase, but the definition is 'Strip' alone, used as a verb; a dive is a disreputable club.
explanation.definitionFit: To divest is to take off or remove clothing or possessions, a formal synonym for the verb strip.

clue.text: With fish, work craftily

blocks.note: W is a standard abbreviation for with
to angle is to fish with rod and line

explanation.surface: Advice on how to do clever handiwork using fish as material.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fish' is a verb here, not the creature.
explanation.definitionFit: To wangle something is to obtain or arrange it by cunning manipulation, which is getting results by crafty means.

clue.text: Volume of goat used by pork pie producer

blocks.note: a billy is a male goat
pork pie is rhyming slang for a lie, so its producer tells lies

explanation.surface: A sales figure for goat meat bought by a maker of pork pies.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Volume' looks like a quantity, but it means a book; pork pie (often shortened to porky) is Cockney rhyming slang for a lie.
explanation.definitionFit: Billy Liar is a 1959 novel by Keith Waterhouse, and a volume is a book, so the title names one.

clue.text: Number Ten is at haste to shift position

indicators.note: letters that shift position are moved around into a different order

blocks.note: the letters taken as written

explanation.surface: Downing Street is in a hurry to change its stance on some policy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Number Ten' reads as the Prime Minister's residence, but 'Number' is the definition: something that numbs, said NUM-er.
explanation.definitionFit: An anaesthetist is the doctor who makes patients numb before surgery, so the cryptic sense of a numbing agent fits.

clue.text: Wearing sandals on vacation, remove socks

indicators.note: whatever is wearing something has it around it, so one piece encloses the other
a word on vacation is emptied of its insides, leaving just its two ends

blocks.note: the first and last letters of sandals
to wipe away a mark is to remove it

explanation.surface: Holiday-makers in sandals are told to take their socks off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'socks' looks like clothing that goes with sandals, but it is a verb: socks someone means hits them hard.
explanation.definitionFit: To sock someone is to punch them, and a swipe is a sweeping blow, so both verbs mean hits.

clue.text: A vocalist’s opening sound

indicators.note: a vocalist's version is what a singer pronounces, so we go by how a word is said

blocks.note: a hole is an opening or gap

explanation.surface: The first note a singer produces when starting a song.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sound' seems to be a noise, but it is the adjective meaning intact or unharmed; HOLE and WHOLE are pronounced the same.
explanation.definitionFit: Safe and sound means unharmed, and whole likewise describes something complete and in good condition.

clue.text: Digs end up hiding crack

indicators.note: in a down entry, going up means reading from bottom to top, so the letters run backwards
to hide something is to keep it inside, so one piece goes within the other

blocks.note: to end something is to stop it
to have a crack at something is to have a shot at it

explanation.surface: Excavations finish by uncovering a fissure, like an archaeologist's site report.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Digs' suggests excavations or lodgings, but it means jibes; 'crack' is an attempt, as in having a crack at something.
explanation.definitionFit: Digs are snide remarks, and potshots are random critical attacks taken at someone, so the two plurals match.

clue.text: Flight impressed those at the rear

indicators.note: the rear of a word is its tail end, so only the closing letter is kept

blocks.note: a mark that is impressed has been stamped into the surface
the last letter of those

explanation.surface: Passengers seated in the back of a plane were delighted by the flight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flight' suggests an air journey, but it means running away; 'impressed' means pressed in, not admired.
explanation.definitionFit: Flight is fleeing, and a stampede is a sudden panicked rush of animals or people running off together.

clue.text: Fine veal stuffed in this?

indicators.note: stuffed letters are crammed in any old way, so they come out in a new order

blocks.note: the letters taken as written

explanation.surface: A cook wonders whether good veal could be stuffed inside this wrapper.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both wordplay and definition: the anagram makes the answer, and the question describes a wrapper that gets stuffed with meat.
explanation.definitionFit: Vine leaves are commonly stuffed with rice and minced meat in Greek and Turkish dolmades, so the question describes one.

clue.text: Stands back, in part sorrowful

indicators.note: only a part of the following words is wanted, a run of consecutive letters inside them
going back means running the letters in the opposite direction

blocks.note: a run of letters spanning the two words

explanation.surface: Someone stands back from a scene, feeling somewhat sad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stands' looks like a verb, but it is a plural noun; the letters straddle 'part' and 'sorrowful' and read right to left.
explanation.definitionFit: Rostra are raised platforms for speakers, the plural of rostrum, and such platforms are also called stands.

clue.text: Staple fare to a top cryptic?

blocks.note: surface reading: a basic, everyday dish served on most dinner plates
setter's reading: the letters of 'to a top' are those of a common vegetable once it has been crushed and jumbled

explanation.surface: A crossword fan wonders whether plain staple food suits the solver of a top-class cryptic.
explanation.walkthrough: This is a reverse anagram: 'to a top' is what you get when the vegetable is mashed, so the answer itself contains the anagram signal and its fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Mashed potato is a basic side dish served with countless meals in Britain, so it is truly staple fare.

clue.text: Rash beginning in someone poorly

indicators.note: the beginning of a word is its first letter, so just that one is used

blocks.note: the first letter of someone
illy is an old adverb meaning badly or poorly

explanation.surface: A skin rash is the first sign that someone is unwell.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rash' looks like a skin complaint, but it is the adjective meaning reckless.
explanation.definitionFit: A rash act is a foolish, thoughtless one, and silly means lacking good sense, so both describe imprudent behaviour.

clue.text: Vehicle’s bodyguards keeping step with it

indicators.note: to keep something is to hold onto it, so one piece is held inside the other

blocks.note: the SS began as Hitler's personal bodyguard unit
a pace is a single step
hip means fashionable, or with it

explanation.surface: Security guards walk alongside a car, matching its speed, as with a presidential motorcade.
explanation.walkthrough: The ’s stands for 'is', joining the definition to the wordplay, and 'with it' is one slang idea, not two words.
explanation.definitionFit: A spaceship is a craft for travelling beyond the atmosphere, so it is a type of vehicle.

clue.text: Delighted flights are so untroubled

blocks.note: first meaning: cheerful and happy
cryptic middle: the inner letters of 'flights', its heart, form a word meaning not heavy
second meaning: free from worry or care

explanation.surface: Happy aircraft passengers report that their journeys were smooth and free of trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: Three readings in one: two plain meanings at either end, and in the middle a joke, since the heart of 'flights', with its outer letters stripped, is LIGHT.
explanation.definitionFit: Light-hearted means carefree and cheerful, matching both the happy sense and the worry-free sense at each end of the clue.

clue.text: Drinks provided in parties, on the rocks

indicators.note: one thing in another sits inside it, so these letters go within the other piece
something on the rocks is wrecked and broken up, so the letters are scrambled

blocks.note: provided that means if
taken as written

explanation.surface: Drinks are handed out at parties, served over ice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on the rocks' sounds like drinks with ice, which suits the surface perfectly, but it signals breaking up the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Aperitifs are alcoholic drinks taken before a meal to stimulate the appetite, so they are a kind of drink.

clue.text: Set eleven without a reserve

indicators.note: without in its old sense means outside, so these pieces sit around the other

blocks.note: to set something down is to put it down
taken as written
a team of eleven players, as in football or cricket, is a side

explanation.surface: A team manager has to field a team of eleven with no substitute on the bench.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' looks like lacking but means outside, and 'reserve' looks like a substitute player but is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To reserve something is to keep it back for later, and to put aside means to save or set it apart.

clue.text: Issues rabble-rousing leader put to the other side

indicators.text: leader put to the other side
indicators.note: the front letter is carried across to the opposite end of the word

blocks.note: sedition is incitement of people against authority

explanation.surface: A demagogue's problems are passed over to the opposition party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'leader' looks like the rabble-rouser himself, but it is the first letter of the word, which moves to the end.
explanation.definitionFit: An issue of a newspaper or magazine is one published copy, and an edition is likewise a single published version.

clue.text: Rudest dancing in underwear, cast if required

indicators.note: dancing letters jump around and end up in a new arrangement
something in something else sits inside it, so one piece goes within the other

blocks.note: taken as written
undies is informal for underwear

explanation.surface: Lewd dancing in underwear, with the performers chosen if the show demands it.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the phrase 'cast if required': performers who go on stage only when a regular actor cannot.
explanation.definitionFit: Understudies learn a lead's part and are put on stage only if needed, so they are actors cast on demand.

clue.text: Submerged in canal, to one’s ears

indicators.note: what reaches one's ears is heard, so the word is judged by its sound

blocks.note: a duct is a channel or canal, as in the ear canal

explanation.surface: Someone has fallen into a canal and gone in right up to their ears.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to one's ears' seems to say how deep the water came, but it means heard.
explanation.definitionFit: To duck someone is to push their head briefly under water, so a person ducked has been submerged.

clue.text: Raw volunteer

blocks.note: first meaning: sore and painful to touch
second meaning: to offer, as in offering a resignation

explanation.walkthrough: 'Raw volunteer' reads as an untrained recruit; split it into two separate meanings of one word.
explanation.definitionFit: A raw wound is tender to touch, and to tender something, such as a bid, is to offer or volunteer it.

clue.text: First course at Pisa, not soup

indicators.note: to be in the soup is to be in a mess, so the letters are jumbled

blocks.note: the letters taken as written

explanation.surface: A diner in Pisa orders a starter but declines the soup.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not soup' looks like a menu choice, but 'not' is part of the letters and 'soup' signals the mix-up.
explanation.definitionFit: Antipasto is the Italian starter of cured meats and vegetables served before the pasta, so it is a first course.

clue.text: Loveless philosopher’s welcomed back to the fold

indicators.note: love is zero, written as the round letter, and less means it is taken away
the back of a word is its end, so only the final letter is used
's stands for has, and to have welcomed someone is to have taken them in

blocks.note: Plato, the Greek philosopher, losing the O for love
the last letter of the

explanation.surface: A thinker abandoned by love is welcomed back into the community.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back to the fold' reads as a homecoming, but 'fold' is the definition and 'back to the' picks out a single letter; love is O, as in tennis scores.
explanation.definitionFit: A pleat is a crease made by doubling fabric over on itself, which is a fold in cloth.

clue.text: Cover that excludes son’s condition

indicators.note: what is excluded is left out, so those letters are dropped

blocks.note: to insure something is to give it cover
S is the standard abbreviation for son

explanation.surface: An insurance policy that does not cover a son's medical condition.
explanation.walkthrough: 'condition' looks like a medical state, but it is a verb meaning to train or accustom.
explanation.definitionFit: To inure someone is to accustom them to hardship, and conditioning is training someone to accept something.

clue.text: Annoyance about working hard finally decreased

indicators.note: about means around, so one piece wraps the other
finally points to the very end, so just the closing letter is kept

blocks.note: ire is anger or annoyance
a machine that is on is working
the last letter of hard

explanation.surface: Someone's irritation at being overworked has finally lessened.
explanation.walkthrough: 'decreased' looks like reduced, but read it as de-creased: with the creases taken out.
explanation.definitionFit: Ironing removes creases from fabric, so something ironed has literally been de-creased, a playful split of the word.

clue.text: Did alarm as dad locked up

blocks.note: pa is an informal word for father
nicked is British slang for arrested and put in a police cell

explanation.surface: A family raised the alarm when their father was arrested and jailed.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain, to be nicked is to be arrested by the police; 'Did alarm' is a past-tense verb phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: To panic someone is to frighten them suddenly, so panicked is the past tense of causing sudden fear.

clue.text: Bogus appeal put in to head off physicist

indicators.note: with its head off, a word loses its first letter
to be put into something is to be placed inside it

blocks.note: Heinrich Hertz, the German physicist, minus his first letter
SA is short for sex appeal

explanation.surface: A fake plea is made to dissuade a scientist from some course of action.
explanation.walkthrough: 'head off' looks like the phrase meaning stop, but it means lose the first letter; SA for sex appeal is a crossword staple.
explanation.definitionFit: Ersatz means an inferior imitation or substitute, so something ersatz is fake, just like something bogus.

clue.text: Deliberate hoax by helter-skelter rides

indicators.note: helter-skelter means in disorderly haste, so the letters land in a confused order

blocks.note: a con is a trick or hoax
taken as written

explanation.surface: A prank was deliberately played near a fairground's helter-skelter slide.
explanation.walkthrough: A helter-skelter is a British fairground ride, a tall spiral slide, which makes 'Deliberate hoax' look like an adjective and noun; 'Deliberate' is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To deliberate is to think something over carefully, and to consider is to weigh it up in the mind.
